I noticed a small issue where display colors were slightly screwed up on wake from suspend (and occasionally, half of the display was blank)

very trivially fixable by switching VTs. I made a script which does it seemlessly on wake 
https://public.hgci.org/software/ELLX/fixes/display-wake/

/lib/systemd/system-sleep/display-fix
```
#!/bin/sh

case $1 in
  post)
    CURRENTVT=$(fgconsole)
    chvt 20
    chvt $CURRENTVT
    ;;
esac
```

Im fully setup. the ipstd was missing systemd service and udev rules so i copyed them over. they needed editing to make them work. instead of `/usr/local/bin/iptsd-...` instead `/usr/bin/iptsd-...` both files come from `iptsd(cloned+built)/build/etc/`. Will auto launch iptsd for you on boot.

`/etc/systemd/systemiptsd@.service`
```diff
[Unit]
Description=Intel Precise Touch & Stylus Daemon
Documentation=https://github.com/linux-surface/iptsd
StopWhenUnneeded=no
BindsTo=%i.device

[Service]
Type=simple
+ ExecStart=/usr/bin/iptsd /%I
```

`/etc/udev/rules.d/50-iptsd.rules`
```diff
SUBSYSTEM=="hidraw", ACTION=="add", TAG+="systemd", \
+ 	PROGRAM="/usr/bin/iptsd-check-device --quiet $env{DEVNAME}", \
	PROGRAM="/bin/systemd-escape --path $env{DEVNAME}", \
	ENV{SYSTEMD_WANTS}+="iptsd@$result.service"
```

it's a bit experimental but I made a full Ubuntu Live ISO geared towards this device: 
~~https://public.hgci.org/software/ELLX/installer/~~ DO not use until I fix audio firmware bug, like in a day or two

A few notes:
* I had a hell of a time getting ubiquity working so I gave up and used calameres. So it's Ubuntu gnome but.. with the kubuntu installer. Sorry!
* Touchpad works in the installer but single touch only. After install I think multitouch should work. If not I screwed up the iptsd service. Good luck
* You *can* infact install to an SD Express card (and it works very well!!!!)! It will boot! But multidrive grub setups dont work. There is a firmware bug that whatever NVMe drive was booted cant see any other NVMe drives. So if you install to SD Express, the "Windows"  button wont work. Instead, to boot windows press "c" to enter the commandline and type "exit". This will trigger the next boot entry, the windows boot manager. 
* Live ISO has no browser. You can type in snap install firefox if you need a browser (Wifi and GPU firmware are in the ISO)
* Sound works. If you put max volume, it triggers a safety though and sound wont work again until you reboot. Sorry. 
* If you have a 64GB ram device, you'll have to type in `cutmem 0x8800000000 0x8fffffffff` into your grub config post install. This is because the hypervisor will panic otherwise on access of the upper 32GB of ram. This is because qualcomm added a fun hypervisor bug. 

Anyways, you can just boot it. Everything works pretty much, except bluetooth. for Bluetooth you have to add a udev rule which sets your mac address. I didn't add this because I dont know how to make it a "random" mac address but only random per install. I'll make a "setup script" for bluetooth if someone is interested though!

Serious work! I'll test this out when I have a spare moment - I'm still working on rewriting hacky patches for more upstreamable quality in hopes that some day this device will be fully supported. Beyond the haptic fix, iptsd has been behaving strangely in general, which has me considering a hard fork (or even rewrite) with a greater focus on touchpad use. If I am being honest, I have been slightly discouraged recognizing touchpad support here will never be as complete as it is on Windows; Microsoft has done a fantastic job locking this hardware into their ecosystem, and as I am no good at math, I struggle to conceptualize what may allow better touch detection/rejection.

I'm not exactly sure what the "vibe coded IPTSD fork" does, but a cursory glance says it does the same thing as this along with other changes that are either completely useless or just slightly useless. It seems to mix up the separation between HID and IPTS, and how those two systems interact within the project. The fork covers more area, which could mean more room for bugs. I haven't had any crashes without the help of suspend with this patch. The other fork does seem to modify the systemd script in a positive way, so that patch you may want to apply as well.

Surface Laptop 7 (ARM / Snapdragon X Elite, 13.8", romulus13) — touchscreen on the second QSPI bus, plus two findings that may save others time

Following up on the work in this thread — the ELLX kernel from @ProgrammerIn-wonderland, the setup guide and camera patches from @bryce-hoehn, the QSPI work from @scuggo, and @orvitpng's findings on iptsd and the heatmaps got me most of the way. On my Surface Laptop 7 with Snapdragon X Elite I now have touchpad, touchscreen, camera, Wi-Fi, GPU, audio, battery and Bluetooth all running. Kernel is the ELLX build for this device, touch via iptsd.

Touchscreen. The QSPI conversion in that kernel covers only &spi19 (the touchpad bus on the Snapdragon's QUP 2 SE 3). There is no fragment for the touchscreen bus at spi@a88000 (QUP 1 SE 2). Adding one — same pattern, compatible = "qcom,geni-spi-qspi", 40 MHz, qcom,qspi-read-opcode = <0xEB>, the GPI DMA node belonging to the QUP 1 wrapper, reset on GPIO 64, IRQ on GPIO 51, child node hid-over-spi — brings it up immediately. On my unit it works through plain hid-multitouch without iptsd, unlike the touchpad. The values come from GTCH (MSHW0460) in the SL7's SSDT; the _DSM there returns the same opcodes and flags as the touchpad, so it is quad SPI as well.

Camera, and a trap worth knowing about on X1E80100. Enabling camss through a runtime device-tree overlay is not sufficient. isp@acb7000 is declared simple-mfd, and its children (the CSIPHYs) only get platform devices if the parent was populated as a bus at boot time. Enable it later and nothing ever populates them, so devm_phy_get() in camss-csiphy.c returns -EPROBE_DEFER — silently, with no reason string recorded, which makes it look like the driver never runs at all. Calling of_platform_populate() on that node from the overlay module fixes it. This applies to any simple-mfd node enabled via overlay, not just on the SL7.

Also, libcamera has no CameraSensorHelper for the SL7's ov02c10 front camera, so the software ISP misreads the gain units. The kernel driver writes the V4L2_CID_ANALOGUE_GAIN value to register 0x3508 unchanged, with OV02C10_ANAL_GAIN_MIN = 0x10 meaning unity gain — so it is AnalogueGainLinear{1, 0, 0, 16}, about twenty lines. That patch is ready and going to the libcamera list; happy to share it here first if anyone wants to test it on their SL7.

Bootloader DTB patches do nothing on this machine. On the Surface Laptop 7, neither GRUB nor systemd-boot gets a modified DTB to the kernel. I verified this with marker properties and by zeroing the DTB file — the system boots unaffected. If earlier device-tree experiments on the SL7 seemed to have no effect, this may well be why. What works is a runtime overlay applied from a small kernel module via of_overlay_fdt_apply().

One practical note for SL7 owners: if touchpad and touchscreen go silent at the same time while both still enumerate cleanly, power the machine off completely rather than rebooting. The 5 V supply for the touch units is only reset by an actual power-down; a warm reboot leaves them wedged. Cost me an hour this morning.

Happy to post the touchscreen overlay source here if that is useful to anyone.

Full writeup with the details, commands and logs: https://horizontblau.de/linux/surface-laptop-7-linux.html

Following up on my earlier post: the Surface Laptop 7 (Snapdragon X Elite, romulus13) is fully working here. Touchpad with gestures and physical click, touchscreen, camera, Wi-Fi, GPU, audio, battery, Bluetooth, suspend.

Almost none of that is my own work. @ProgrammerIn-wonderland's kernel packages, @scuggo's quad-SPI implementation for spi-geni-qcom, @bryce-hoehn's setup guide and camera patches, @orvitpng's account of the three touchpad modes and the heatmap route, @alex-lentz's iptsd fork — I mostly assembled what was already there. Thank you.

Three things I can add in return:

1. The shipped iptsd binary cannot start on this hardware. It crashes with SIGILL on every invocation, including --help, before touching any device — inconsistent branch-protection flags between the package's components, so an indirect jump lands on an address without a valid BTI landing pad. objcopy --remove-section=.note.gnu.property on a copy makes it run; rebuilding from source with consistent -mbranch-protection=standard fixes it properly. If anyone here concluded "iptsd doesn't work on the SL7", this may well be why — it never got to run.

2. Hiding the raw device needs to be selective. Once iptsd runs, its uinput device and the kernel's compete. A udev rule with LIBINPUT_IGNORE_DEVICE=1 on ID_PATH=platform-88c000.spi-cs-0 fixes that — but it must also match ID_INPUT_TOUCHPAD=="1", because the same controller reports the physical button through a separate node (spi 045E:0C77 Mouse). Hide that one too and you lose clicking entirely.

3. @alex-lentz's fork is what brings the button back. With upstream 3.1.0 the physical click never reaches the virtual device — once iptsd switches modes, the controller stops sending ordinary HID button reports and upstream doesn't forward the state. The fork's "button debounce and palm-suppression click leak" change fixes exactly that. Dragging windows works now.

Also: @valpackett was right about stubble — Ubuntu's generic kernel carries 33 .dtbauto sections plus .hwids, the ELLX kernel has none. My "bootloaders can't pass a DTB" claim was wrong and is corrected in the writeup.

Touchscreen overlay source and the full recipe: https://horizontblau.de/linux/surface-laptop-7-linux.html — happy to post any of it inline here if that's more useful.

Is the raw device not quiet once iptsd switches on the microslop custom protocol? What does it keep reporting? Does the entire basic mouse reporting keep running?

You were right, and my wording was wrong. I measured it on a healthy touchpad: ten seconds of steady swiping plus a physical click, reading every evdev node of the SPI HID device in the same window.

With iptsd running, all five kernel nodes emit exactly zero events — the three unnamed ABS collections, "Mouse" and "Touchpad" alike. Only iptsd's uinput device reports: 3365 events, ABS_MT_POSITION_X/Y, BTN_TOUCH, BTN_LEFT.

With iptsd stopped, the same swipe gives 2380 events on the "Mouse" node: REL_X=718, REL_Y=758, BTN_LEFT 8 press/release.

So basic mouse reporting does not keep running alongside iptsd — the raw device goes quiet the moment iptsd switches protocols, exactly as you expected. Nothing competes. My "compete" claim was unmeasured and is simply wrong; I'm correcting it in the write-up.

One detail I did not expect: the kernel's "Touchpad" node (hid-multitouch, ABS_MT_*, INPUT_PROP_PRESSUREPAD) is silent in both runs. It is never fed at all — the device only ever speaks basic mouse or the vendor protocol. That also explains an earlier observation of mine where BTN_LEFT was declared on that node but never arrived: I had been watching a node the device never serves.

For what it's worth, the rule I use is already selective — it hides only the node udev classes as ID_INPUT_TOUCHPAD, and explicitly re-exposes the Mouse node, which is what leaves a working pointer when iptsd is not running.

Two follow-ups on the touchpad controller wedge (ELLX tree, 7.0.0-rc4+, romulus13).

**spi-hid registers neither .shutdown nor .pm**, so the controller loses its 5 V rail mid-operation at poweroff instead of being placed in reset first, as ACPI _PS3 does. A systemd unit now pulls GPIO 120 low on ExecStop, waits 10 ms, then unbinds spi_hid — spi_hid_power_down() selects the reset state and calls regulator_disable(), so the rail drops after reset. Measured on a real shutdown: gap 14–15 ms, regulator afterwards `state=disabled num_users=0`. Unproven as a cure; it addresses how the controller gets into the state, not how to get it out.

**One owner per line.** In x1e80100-microsoft-romulus.dtsi both `spi19_hid0_reset_{de,}assert` list `pins = "gpio65", "gpio120"`, while `vreg_ts_5p0` also owns gpio65 via `gpio = <&tlmm 65 0>` — and it is one of only two regulators in that file without `regulator-boot-on`.

    +       regulator-boot-on;              /* vreg_ts_5p0 */
    -       pins = "gpio65", "gpio120";     /* both reset states */
    +       pins = "gpio120";

Regulator tracepoints on a test boot: vreg_ts_5p0 enables at 1.609 s, first input device at 5.297 s, no regulator_disable in between. Control in the same boot: the untouched vreg_ts2_5p0 enables only at 5.597 s, from the udev worker at probe. Interrupt rate unchanged.

Full write-up with all measurements: https://horizontblau.de/linux/surface-laptop-7-linux.html
